The Disarmament and International Security Committee, the first committee for the 81st session of the General Assembly, is called to order. Distinguished delegates, at the outset, allow me to extend a very warm welcome to all the delegations participating in this committee's deliberations at the current session of the General Assembly. I also take this opportunity to state how honored I am and deeply indebted to all of you for the privilege and distinction you have bestowed upon my country and on me personally in electing me as the chair of this very important committee of the General Assembly. I shall do my utmost in full collaborations with other members of the current Bureau to discharge my responsibilities in a manner to ensure that our work is carried out efficiently and that our endeavors meet with success. Before proceeding to the matters at hand, I am sure that I speak on behalf of the entire membership of this Committee in commending Ambassador Maurizio Massari of Italy for the skillful and effective manner in which he conducted the proceedings of the First Committee at its 80th session. I should also like to pay tribute to other members of the previous Bureau for all their hard work in ensuring the success of the sessions. Before proceeding further, I would like to remind delegation that when elections of the Bureau members of the First Committee for the 81st session of the GA took place on June 2nd, 2026, our nominations remain pending for vice chair from the group of Latin American and Caribbean states. It is my pleasure to inform the committee that from that group, the nominations of Mr. Clarkson, Duberry of Antigua and Barbuda, have been received for the positions of the vice-chair of the first committee for this session. Since no other candidate has been nominated for this position, may I take it that the committee wishes to elect by acclamation Mr. Clarkston DuVernay of Antigua and Barbuda to the position of Vice-Chair of the First Committee at its 81st session. I hear no objections. It is so decided. I warmly congratulate Mr. DuVernay on his election. I'm confident that I can rely on the support of all the members of the Bureau, namely the three Vices, Mr. Clarkson Duverri of Antigua and Barbuda, Mr. Arsen Kotanyan of Armenia, and Mr. Fajal Abdel Jameel Salim Mohammed of Sudan, as well as the Rapporteur, Ms. Kim van der Sloot of the Kingdom of Netherlands. I have no doubt that the Committee will benefit tremendously from their collective wisdom. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, as noted in UN Journal, the meeting today will address the organizations of the work of the Committee and will include a debate on the working methods of the Committee and program planning. We will first turn to the organizations of the work of the Committee for this session. The committee has before it the document A/C.1/81/1, containing the 21 agenda items allocated to the committee by the General Assembly at its second plenary meeting on 11 September 2026. The committee also has before it the documents is less C1/81/CIP1 and CIP2. Document CIP1 contains the committee's proposed program of work and timetables for 2026. CIP2 is the draft indicative timetable for the structured discussion of the specific subjects on the adopted thematic approach and determined and international security agenda items. Before examining these documents one by one, with the Committee's indulgence, I should like to inform delegations of the manner in which I intend to conduct our meetings. In order to make full use of the time and conference services made available to the Committee, with your cooperation and support, I shall convene the meetings of the Committee 00 a.m. and 3:00 p.m. sharp. Similarly, I shall adjourn the meetings punctually 00 p.m. and 6:00 p.m. respectively. I therefore appeal to all the speakers, especially the first three speakers at a given meeting, to kindly be present in the conference room on time. I should also like to remind members that the Assembly has decided to continue its practice during the sessions of waiving the requirement that at least one quarter of the members be present to declare a Main Committee meeting open and permit the debate to proceed. The Assembly made these recommendations on the understanding that Such a departure from the rules did not involve any permanent change in the provisions of the Rule 108 of its Rules of Procedure. Returning to the allocation of agenda items allocated to the committee is contained in document A/C.1/81/1. I would like to highlight the following. This is to enhance discussions of evaluations, planning, budgeting, and monitoring reports. As noted earlier, the Committee will consider items 124 and 139 jointly later this morning. The Secretariat has prepared a note issued is document A/C.1/81/INF/4 under the two items. Distinguished delegates, let us now turn our attention to the Committee's proposed programme of work and timetable as outlined in document A/C.1/81/CRP.1. This document is based on General Assembly decisions 80/515 of 1 December 2025. But in view of the current liquidity crisis facing the organizations, requiring the committee to reduce the number of meetings this session, it reflects the proposals of the current bureau not to meet on October 1, nor on 4 to 6 November. while having an additional meeting on 29 October in the afternoon. The Committee will maintain its established practice of conducting its work in three phases, namely a general debate on all agenda items, thematic discussions on specific subjects, and final reaction on all draft proposals. It will also conclude its work by 3rd November for a total of 28 meetings. After careful and long considerations, the Bureau is proposing a program that fully maintains the required number of meetings for the Committee's general debate and the action phase, while once again including the debate on the working methods of the Committee and program planning in today's meeting. For the best use of the resources, allocated to the committee. Mr. Chair, the United States would like to thank the Bureau, the Secretariat, and you for your efforts to prepare the program of work for this year's first committee. We acknowledge that some improvements have been made, and we appreciate the Chair's efforts to move the Committee in a more efficient direction. The draft before us is an improvement over where this process began, but let us be candid, it falls short of what is needed. Last year, the United States made clear that First Committee could and should operate more efficiently. The 2025 session proved that point. The committee completed its work in 20 business days, effectively four working weeks, even with holidays interrupting the schedule. We saw no loss of participation, no reduction in the number of interventions, and no evidence that the committee's mandate suffered in any way, to the contrary. The data showed that the work got done. That experience should have settled the matter. Apparently, it did not. Despite repeated calls from the United States and broad support from many delegations in this room for a shorter, more disciplined schedule, the committee still has not embraced the level of reform that the moment requires. At a time when the United Nations faces sustained budget pressure, this body should not defend excess time, excess cost, and outdated habits simply because that is how things were done in the past. The committee should align its schedule with the actual work required and not preserve inefficiency as a matter of convenience. Mr. Chair, The United States remains committed to a more effective, accountable, and results-oriented United Nations, one that advances international peace and security and respects the resources member states provide. That means shorter sessions, tighter speaking limits, fewer unnecessary rights of reply, and a serious movement toward running more technical resolutions on a biennial or triennial basis. While many countries have taken this request seriously, others have not. So, Mr. Chair, let me be clear. This year, the United States will not block consensus on the adoption of the agenda or program of work. We will not call for a vote. We will not offer amendments. We urge other member states likewise to oppose any proposals to make changes to move us in the wrong direction. But let me be clear, we will continue to fight for reform and expect to see additional reductions next year, including materially shorter session and stronger efficiency measures. In that sense, we are putting the committee on notice now. Incremental gestures will no longer be enough. The time for serious reform is here. Thank you, Mr. Chair.

Improvements we can already identify include encouraging the trend for more concise statements, stricter limits on speaking, greater transparency in procedural decisions of the Committee, and a more focused meeting structure. In addition, and consistent with the GA resolutions mentioned earlier, member states contributing to the committee's work should continue to review and, where possible, streamline their approach towards overall numbers of resolutions they propose each year, along with the periodicity of some resolutions that are considered, especially those that have remained largely static for many years. The high volume of resolutions each session ultimately contributes to a diluted focus and more superficial discussions. This creates the risk that we fail to adequately grapple with the key issues of the day, and it can stretch and even exceed the resources of smaller delegations to meaningfully engage. We also further highlight the importance of striving for gender parity in the work of the Committee, including among speakers and panelists in high-level and thematic meetings.
