However, this measure should not affect the process of informal consultations, bearing in mind that informal consultations make it possible to reconcile positions and explore pathways towards the desired consensus. We hope, however, that when rights of reply are exercised, they do not become an extension of national statements. My third point, Mexico supports efforts to make more effective use of the resources allocated to the General Assembly. This in line with commitments regarding the UNAG initiative. With this in mind, we have reviewed our own initiatives and moved to two or three year cycles for them. We've sought to avoid superfluous mandates or reports which provide very little or very scant added value, we once again appeal to other delegations to consider similar measures. Mexico is of the view that genuine revitalization cannot be limited to simply reorganizing the First Committee's timetable. We must comprehensively review disarmament machinery and the way in which its various components interact. We are concerned that three decades have elapsed since the last time that the CD was fully able to discharge its mandate. This year, That is the Conference on Disarmament. This year, the UNDC was not able to adopt substantive conclusions. Finally, any substantive amendment should be discussed in an inclusive way and sufficiently in advance. And ideally, this should take place before the organizational sessions. With that in mind, we welcome the informal discussion that was held in April. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Mexico. Now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Poland.

Hello. Thank you, Mr. Chair. At first, let me congratulate you on the assumption of the chairmanship of the first committee. Please be assured that you can count on Poland's full support. And with many thanks for your strenuous efforts so far, let me chip into the working methods debate with three points. Firstly, Reducing the number of meetings and streamlining the session should be seen as a joint measure implemented to save time, improve the effectiveness and the general functioning of this committee. The view that fewer meetings would lead to a greater burden for smaller delegations is inexplicable to us. We see the reductions as a chance to reallocate time for further involvement and prepare better for other segments of the session, also to work on the resolutions that are the key results of the committee's work. After all, we work together on these texts and the more informal time we have to discuss them, the better shape they have. Therefore, the ideas put forward by the Bureau, with the strong preference to streamline further, certainly improve the Committee's work. Chair, given that last year we finished ahead of schedule, with the liquidity measures in full force, coming to business as usual would be simply logical. That view was largely echoed in April, when 120 delegations attended the intersessional meeting And of approximately 30 that took the floor, only one was openly against reductions. It was Russia. The same Russia that has already started obstructing the session today. Chair, secondly, Poland supports clustering the exercise of rights of reply statements and regrets that this idea will not be implemented this session. RRR interventions are very often repetitive and ill-conceived. Even though an intervention constitutes an inherent right of a state, it does not mean that one should abuse the right and treat the RRR segment as an opportunity to deliver another or sometimes the same statement. RRR's aim is to respond, not to repeat. Therefore, clustering and shortening these interventions is a convenient way forward that reduces the level of repetitiveness and debate fatigue, issues about which many states complain. Thirdly and finally, I would like to draw your attention to the figures presented by the Secretariat in April. Last year, approximately 40% of 1C resolutions were subject to non-substantive updates. In other words, almost half of the texts were technical rollovers. Let me be clear, adding a number and date to the resolution does not amount to constructive engagement in disarmament talks. It preserves legacy structures. That political objective is understandable but does not have to be fulfilled every year. We urge delegations planning to table technical rollovers to biennialize or triennialize them. Chair, to conclude, let's build on good practices, like Franco-German non-paper or internal bureau ideas, so that we work effectively rather than aimlessly. As a former bureau member, I wish you and your team best of luck. You can count on us. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Poland. Now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of El Salvador.

Thank you, Chair. El Salvador is grateful for the opportunity to once again contribute to this debate. We regret the fact that we were unable to adopt all the provisions of the programme of work. We encourage the holding of more consultations on it. On working methods, in recent years, my delegation has consistently raised the need to move towards a first committee that is more inclusive, efficient and streamlined. We have supported the biennialisation and triennialisation of resolutions, the merging of mandates when possible and the promotion of omnibus resolutions. We wish to emphasize this year, particularly that last point, El Salvador fully recognizes the sovereign prerogative of all member states to present draft resolutions for the consideration of the General Assembly. At the same time, as we have indicated since 2023, we believe it's important to continue contemplating situations in which resolutions are presented on one single issue that contains significant overlaps. The overlapping and the proliferation of resolutions and mandates increases the workload of the committee, and it makes it difficult for all delegations to participate effectively. That's particularly true for small delegations such as my own. As such, we're of the view that greater coordination between resolution proposers will not only streamline our work, but it will also preserve the coherence of the processes that unfold within this Committee. Chair, Member States have worked tirelessly to, in various fora, build spaces for dialogue and cooperation. On occasion, after complex negotiating processes, We are of the view that it is important for the work of the first committee to strengthen these fora and to allow them to fully discharge the mandates that have been entrusted to them. With that in mind, we encourage those proposing resolutions that are tackling similar issues to step up the pace of consultations and explore as far as possible, when the circumstances allow, to merge their proposals into common texts. That will serve to avoid overlap and to facilitate broader participation of members as well as to foster more coherent implementation of the mandates agreed upon. We recognize that there are substantive differences between states and that achieving that goal will not always be possible. It is precisely for that reason that we believe that coordination, dialogue and flexibility between those proposing texts should be promoted as part of our working methods. This is particularly true when we already have established fora and mandates within which we can continue to tackle these differences of opinion. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of El Salvador. Now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Belarus.

Mr. Chairman, first and foremost, we wish to take this opportunity to thank you for your willingness and readiness to continue the discussion of the program of work of the fifth committee of the first committee we thank you for your flexibility so as to ensure that the views of all delegations are born in mind in this important matter we believe that the reconsideration of the principles and working methods of the committee of the first committee is possible exclusively on the basis of a consensus in order to genuinely improve and streamline the work of the committee there's a need to conduct a broad informal consultations ahead time on any new initiatives, which are geared towards changing the parameters for its operations. I now turn to the broadly discussed matter of reduction in volume of meetings, reduction in time for meetings of the First Committee. We do not agree that this will in any way enhance the effectiveness and efficiency of our negotiations organ. For last year, reduction in the volume of meetings resulted in a dearth of time for comprehensive substantive discussions and a reduction in the volume of agreed-upon documents and heightened tensions. Furthermore, this is exceedingly uncomfortable for smaller delegations, as we already saw and heard from statements in this hall, including for the Belarusian delegation. We have a profound, in-depth, substantive dialogue. Such a dialogue requires time, and this is something which we all know well. Instead of an in-depth professional analysis of problems, frequently we have to limit ourselves to condensed statements. And these kinds of so-called these savings undermine international security, arms control, and nonproliferation. To conclude, Mr. Chairman, I to highlight two important, as we see it, components. The first is as follows. Any initiatives to change the frequency of resolutions submitted need not encroach upon the sovereign right of delegations to submit documents under their discretion. At their discussion, another important issue has to do with the deadline for the tabling of resolutions. We propose that this be shifted to the third week of the session. This will ease the work of smaller delegations and will provide sufficient time for reaching agreement on the documents. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Belarus. Now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of South Africa.

Thank you, Chairperson. South Africa aligns with the statement delivered on behalf of the African Group. Chairperson, South Africa also supports the proposed provisional program of work and indicative timetable. We would like to reiterate our support for efforts to improve the working methods of the committee in order to ensure that work is conducted in an effective and efficient manner. We note the proposal on time allocations. And as indicated, we believe that these measures can contribute to the efficient use of the committee's time, as demonstrated by the 80th session of the committee. At the same time, such allocation should not create an imbalance between the consideration of procedural issues and substantive matters, which in our view warrant adequate time and attention. South Africa supports the consideration of the biennialization and/or triennialization of resolutions, particularly those that primarily contain technical updates. However, we do not consider that decisions regarding the periodicity of resolutions should be based on a uniform approach. Rather, each resolution should be considered on its own merits, taking into account each subject matter, relevance, intended purpose, and current developments. Chairperson, another important matter on the working methods is that of transparency. Over its previous two sessions, the Committee has been able to create more space for transparency to thrive through the implementation of Decision 79/516 on information on requests for votes, which was adopted by consensus. South Africa therefore affirms the continued validity of this decision and supports its sustained implementation as an important and constructive measure for building trust and confidence among Member States. We wish to restate that the purpose of this decision is neither to name and shame Member States, nor to restrict their right to call a vote. It is intended to assist delegations by providing timely information on requests for votes and provide Member States with an opportunity to engage each other on issues of concern and common interest. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of South Africa. Now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Lithuania. Microphone, please, to Lithuania.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. It is never too late to congratulate you on your election as Chair of the First Committee and to congratulate the other members of the Bureau. You can count on Lithuania's full support and cooperation. Lithuania reiterates its appreciation for the efforts of the Chair and the Bureau to make the Committee's work more efficient. Without repeating myself, we welcome the efficiency measures introduced, and hopefully, we will be able to agree on them quite soon. Lithuania still believes that there remains room for further improvements to the Committee's efficiency. Let me briefly touch upon a few areas. First, the length of the programme of work and related streamlining measures. Measures such as enforced time limits, shorter sessions and early informal engagement have proven beneficial. Reported increase participation in 2025 with a higher number of speakers in formal debates demonstrated the value of these efforts. The Committee's successful completion of its work ahead of the schedule during the previous session suggests that further efficiencies could be explored. provided that sufficient time is preserved for substantive discussions and informal consultations. Second, the right of reply. While it remains an important procedural tool, it should not be used to circumvent agreed speaking limits or to prolong interventions through lengthy exchanges, especially that are not directly relevant to the Committee's mandate and agenda. We therefore support the time limits for rights of reply that are proportionate to the speaking times allocated during the corresponding debate. Third, Lithuania would encourage continued reflection on the periodicity of resolutions. We encourage Member States to consider whether certain resolutions that undergo only technical updates from year to year could benefit from alternative periodicities or where appropriate to use of decisions while preserving substantive engagement on the issue. We also see scope for consolidating closely related resolutions where appropriate. Such steps could help reduce both committees workload and associated financial burden. At the time of growing security challenges and continued financial constraints facing the United Nations, our efficiency should be measured by the quality of our outcomes rather than the length of our interventions. Lithuania remains open to discussing. We appreciate the contributions made by delegations to this discussion and remain open to discuss further improvements in the future. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Lithuania. Now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Russian Federation.

Mr. Chairman. we firmly believe in the relevance and importance of traditional working methods of the First Committee, and we see no need in their revision. The relevant approaches have been set out in detail in the position paper of the Russian delegation, which was circulated among all United Nations member states, and this specifically pertains to the First Committee's working methods. We call upon all delegations to familiarize themselves with this. I now turn to the duration of statements. There is a need to preserve the traditional duration so as to ensure that delegations have the opportunity to engage in a substantive matter agenda items of the first committee and to seek to arrive at mutually acceptable solutions for real, not imaginary, problems in the area of international security, arms control, nonproliferation, disarmament. I now turn to the right to reply, which certain delegations resort to. The main reason, based on statistics in recent years, the main reason is precisely politicized, deliberately factually incorrect statements which are emanating precisely from those states who so ardently call for limitations on this right and calling for our delegations to be stripped of the opportunity to respond to obvious attacks. Consequently, through a simple resolution to the problem is as follows: such countries that call for restrictions on the right to reply, they simply can not engage in politicized, clearly false allegations and statements targeting other participants. Enhancement of the effectiveness and efficiency would be facilitated by a thorough, good-faith preparatory work, including the conduct of open-ended consultations on all new initiatives at the committee. At the same time, it is important for states not to impose deliberately non-consensus-based ideas, which result in further divisions in the international community, rather for them to seek a positive agenda. They wanted for the goal to be merger of efforts. This would help to enhance the effectiveness and efficiency of the relevant initiatives. I now turn to the proposals of a transition to a biennial or triennial basis of the draft resolutions. We would like to underscore that such ideas should not undermine the sovereign rights of member states to advance their proposals to determine the content and the periodicity of the resolutions and General Assembly decisions, and the attempts to arbitrarily limit to member states' opportunity to present documents and the advancement of their initiatives in the area of arms control disarmament and nonproliferation are unacceptable in our view. The relevant decisions need to be taken by the sponsors of the resolution independently based upon their specific circumstances. Thank you for your attention.
I thank the distinguished representative of Russian Federation. Now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Belgium.

Mr. Chairman, Belgium reiterates our words of gratitude for your efforts, which are geared towards improving the working methods of the First Committee. We regret the impossibility this morning of adopting a working program of work. In light of a dense agenda and constraints as a result of growing resource constraints, it is incumbent upon us to see to it that the First Committee become an effective, efficient forum that can dedicate more time to substantive discussion seeking concrete solutions. We support the initiative proposed by the Bureau for the working program of work for this session, specifically reduction in the overall duration of this session, as well as proposals to limit the duration of time statements, as well as to strictly cut off microphones at the expiration of time limits? There is some leeway, and to that end, we believe that there is room, rather, for improvement in the operations of the Committee. To that end, we would like to recall our support for the proposals in the Franco-German non-paper that was proposed. This includes a five-minute statement for national statements, eight minutes for statements on behalf of groups during the general debate, to second, a more selective approach the submission of draft resolutions by prioritizing texts which include new mandates or substantive modifications, and third, to prioritize biannualization or triannualization of resolutions, and fourth, the merger of thematic clusters six and seven. Lastly, we believe that the question of rights of reply also warrants particular attention. Belgium can accept keeping things unchanged in the spirit of compromise this year, but we would like next year to have an organization of rights of response be held every other day rather than on a daily basis, as well as the grouping together rights of response at the end of each thematic cluster during the thematic cluster, and stricter limitations on speaking times during rights of response. We believe that three minutes for the first statement intervention, two minutes for the second intervention is sufficient. As was mentioned, we do not support some delegations' view that this will have an impact on trust among states. will result in an increase in the number of resolutions voted upon. We believe that bringing together all of these measures will help to significantly reduce the duration of work of the First Committee to four weeks, while at the same time maintaining their quality, transparency, and inclusive nature. And this will help to free up more time for informal discussions as well. We stand ready to engage and pursue dialogue with all delegations in order to identify pragmatic and consensus-based reforms to help the First Committee become more effective and efficient. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Belgium. Now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Italy.

Mr. President, let me reiterate again my congratulations for your important role and that of the Bureau. We are convinced that working methods focused on efficiency, pragmatism, and oriented on results are the best possible way to make the work of this committee relevant and fruitful. Streamlining working methods does not mean neglecting the importance of the discussions carried out. It means focusing on them with a-- focusing them on what is most urgent to achieve progress in the field of disarmament and international security. And exactly by allowing every delegation to have the full chance to express its views, while at the same time preserving a smooth and really interactive debate, real exchange of views, in which the positions of every niche of the delegations can be better highlighted, understood in the very essence, and receive full attention they deserve on a ground of true parity. During the last session of the first committee last year, it was proved that putting together streamlined working methods and full inclusivity of the debate is possible and is fruitful.

Therefore, we are very grateful

to you and to this Bureau for having proposed efficiency measures that we fully support. Thank you, Mr. President.
I thank the distinguished representative of Italy. Now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Switzerland.

Mr. Chairman, Switzerland would like to thank you, as well as the Bureau and the Secretariat, for the efforts undertaken to prepare the programme of work and the working methods for the 81st session of the First Committee. Switzerland supports the measures put in place, both with regard to the programme of work and the working methods. We consider them to be useful steps towards ensuring the effective organisation of our work. Going forward, we believe it would be useful to finalise the arrangements for organising the work of the first committee sufficiently in advance in order to facilitate the planning of the participation of member state delegations. In this spirit, Switzerland encourages the continuation of these efforts during the next session, and we wish to put forward the following three suggestions. First and foremost, we encourage delegations to consider biennializing or even triennializing resolutions whose content does not undergo substantial changes from one year to the next, without prejudice to the possibility of reconsidering them in light of new developments. This is merely an encouragement. Second, We encourage the strict and consistent application of speaking times, including where appropriate by cutting off the microphone, applied equally to all delegations. This measure would help to ensure fairness amongst speakers and respect for the programme of work. These measures, in our view, should go hand in hand with preserving the inclusive and substantive nature of the First Committee's debates. Third, we encourage further consideration in a more in-depth way of the practice of the right to reply. We take note of the measures introduced in this regard, and we appreciate the efforts undertaken We encourage the chairmanship to continue to engage with delegations in order to identify for future sessions a way to make this practice even more effective and targeted, while fully respecting the rights of all delegations. In this regard, the proposal to group rights of reply at the end of each thematic debate, rather than at the end of each day, in our view, is constructive. Switzerland looks forward to continuing this discussion with the chair and all delegations. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Switzerland. Now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Nicaragua.

Chair, we congratulate you and the members of the Bureau on your election. You can count on the full support of Nicaragua. in terms of constructively contributing to the Committee's work. Nicaragua is of the view that it is pivotal to preserve the intergovernmental, inclusive and representative nature of the first Committee. We should guarantee that all Member States are able to fully and equally participate in the First Committee's work. We acknowledge the financial difficulties currently faced by our organization. As such, in our view, it is important to ensure that measures adopted make it possible to preserve the space necessary for dialogue, negotiation and the effective participation of all Member States. The First Committee broaches particularly sensitive issues for international peace and security. As such, we reiterate that it is vital to have sufficient time for general and thematic debates. Consultations between delegations and the exercise of the right of reply foster substantive exchange, and that is helpful in terms of building understanding. Moreover, of the view, any substantive amendment to the committee's working methods should, in our view, be examined in a balanced fashion without stymying debate and while preserving fully the prerogatives of member states, as well as seeking always to achieve consensus. All member states to sovereign right to propose resolutions must be preserved. Consultation should be allowed to preserve the inclusive nature of the Committee's work. We continue to trust that your Chair will provide us with important input as we seek to bolster the First Committee's ability to effectively discharge its mandate. We hope that you will allow us to ensure the First Committee remains a vital space for discussion on disarmament, we will continue to constructively foster a process of negotiation rooted in dialogue, mutual respect, multilateralism, consensus, and the equitable participation of all States. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Nicaragua. Now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Thailand.

Mr. Chair, as this is the first time my delegation takes the floor, allow me to congratulate you and the members of the Bureau on your election. This is a pleasure to see a close friend from the Asia-Pacific at the helm. You have Thailand's full support. We also thank the Secretariat for providing the statistics and information that inform our work. Mr. Chair, Thailand welcomes the continued efforts to improve the work of this committee. The 80th session showed that the efficiency and inclusivity can reinforce one another. Efficiency should serve substance, not replace it, and should preserve attention to longstanding priorities, including nuclear disarmament. Let me reflect on some points raised on the program of work. We concur with Norway that the streamlined arrangements should continue for another year before we assess them again. One year of statistics is a starting point, not a proof of success. That assessment must include the views of smaller delegations. Senegal's experience of engaging in only two thematic discussions last year, fewer than before, deserves our attention. Mr. Chair, reform begins with how we Member States work. We see three practical steps. First, earlier and more inclusive engagement. Early circulation of drafts helps build wider support. Consultations in Geneva and Vienna are valuable. Virtual formats could connect them with New York, home to the widest membership, including smaller delegations represented only here. Participation means ownership. Second, more focused reporting. Consolidated and targeted requests for views would ease the burden on smaller delegations. This could generate more responses and add value to their reports. Third, a voluntary review of the periodicity of resolutions. Texts with only technical updates could be presented every two or three years. This would free time for issues requiring deeper discussion, while fully respecting every state's right to submit proposals. Mr. Chair, improving our working methods is an ongoing process. We should continue good practices such as speaking time limits and transparency on requests for recorded votes, and pursue measures that enjoy broad convergence. These include issues such as further rationalizing the speaking time limit, merging thematic clusters, strengthening the disarmament machinery. Progress ultimately depends on political will, but there is room for practical improvement through inclusive consultations with all stakeholders. My delegation would welcome continued intercessional discussions, should you and the Bureau see merit in it. Thailand stands ready to contribute. I thank you, Mr. Chair.
I thank the distinguished representative of Thailand. Now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Zimbabwe.

Thank you, Chair. Zimbabwe congratulates you, Chair, and your Bureau on your election to lead the First Committee during its 81st session. Please be assured of Zimbabwe's full support and constructive engagement. Zimbabwe aligns with the statement delivered by the African Group and adds the following in a national capacity. Distinguished delegates, the prevailing international security environment has made it more imperative for the First Committee to fulfill its mandate in line with the Charter of the United Nations. With the ongoing qualitative and quantitative arms race that appears to be underway, Zimbabwe underscores that the First Committee has an even greater role today to refocus global attention on the need for general and complete disarmament under strict and effective international control. Chair, Zimbabwe welcomed the inter-sessional informal discussion on the working methods of the First Committee held in April 2026 and noted the various positions expressed by Member States. In that vein, we maintain the view that time limits for national and group statements and for rights of reply should not be further reduced, as this may diminish the quality and substance of exchanges. Drawing from the position paper of the Russian Federation, which was circulated by the Secretariat in August 2026, Zimbabwe adds its voice to the view that member states should not be arbitrarily restricted from submitting documents and promoting their initiatives in the sphere of arms control, disarmament, and non-proliferation. On another note, Zimbabwe continue to support General Assembly decision 79516, which has enabled the identification of Member States calling for a vote in the interest of transparency and dialogue. Finally, we reiterate that measures that were implemented due to financial crisis should not remain in force beyond the necessary timeframe. Let me conclude by extending appreciation to the Bureau for its steadfast efforts to improve the Committee's working methods. We also appreciate the dedicated support of the Secretariat. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Zimbabwe. Now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Cuba.

Thank you, Chair. We congratulate you once again. on your election as Chair of the First Committee. We also congratulate the Vice-Chairs that will accompany you during this session. We wish you every success as you discharge your mandate. We take note of the proposal on the table regarding the working methods for the 81st session. We also note the comments made by several delegations on the working methods assessed. In view of the Organization's current financial situation, it is necessary to guarantee a sensible use of resources available. However, these measures should not stymie the full and effective participation of all Member States in the work of the Committee, neither should they affect the exercise of their rights. In the current international context, marked by growing challenges to international peace and security, it is crucial to preserve adequate space for substantive, inclusive and transparent dialogue on disarmament and non-proliferation. Like other delegations, we are currently concerned by the reduction to the number of meetings as well as to the time available for statements during the general debate. These measures should be... and remain strictly exceptional and should not set a precedent for future sessions. We recognise, against this backdrop, efforts made by the Bureau under Nepal's leadership to facilitate an organisational process that can allow the Commission to adequately discharge its mandate. We reiterate the importance that my delegation attaches to maintaining the exercise of having rights of reply at the end of every day of thematic discussions. This practice will serve to guarantee a balanced exchange of views and the effective exercise of the rights of all Member States. Chair, regarding the proposals to reduce biennialised or triennialised resolutions, And regarding the recommendations regarding technical roll-overs, this measure should not be used as an economic means to limit the rights of a State or a group of States, including the NAM, to present draft resolutions or decisions. Neither should it be used as a measure to determine their content or their frequency. We are staunchly committed to multilateralism, disarmament and international security, as well as the efficiency of the First Committee. That efficiency should be measured according to its ability to promote substantive participation and the full participation of all member states and its ability to seek mutually acceptable solutions. We are ready to constructively participate in all the committee's work. Thank.
I thank the distinguished representative of Cuba. Now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Pakistan.

Thank you, Chair. Pakistan recognizes the First Committee as a unique, most inclusive, and universal forum on arms control, disarmament, and international security. Entrusted by the General Assembly to carry out on its behalf critical deliberations on a range of regional and international security issues, The First Committee provides an important opportunity to all Member States to take stock of developments in key disarmament areas across the globe. We support the continued efforts to promote efficiency as well as smooth and effective functioning of the First Committee. In this respect, we offer the following points. First, we should be clear-headed about the purposes and overarching goals of any efficiency exercise. All efforts and their outcomes should aim to preserve and further enhance the salient and strategic nature of the first committee. Second, we must strike a balance between cost-cutting and promoting efficiency while fostering effectiveness and productivity. We should avoid the urge to turn this solely as a mechanical exercise of progressive cut down, rather should ensure optimal level of resources. Third, Any exercise should strive for the widest possible views of member states in transparent and inclusive manner, and decisions should ideally be taken by a consensus. This would ensure the buy-in of all member states in these important endeavors. Ultimately, our overall goal is to further enhance common understanding of all issues, including on working methods and allocation of precious time and resources. With the above in view, we suggest that member states may initiate a dedicated in-depth exercise of these issues in a comprehensive manner, where deliberations and decisions are taken holistically, inclusively, and transparently. While any decision in this respect is the member state's responsibility, the secretariat may be requested to prepare a comprehensive conference paper providing a detailed background of all related issues with historical development and evolution of the first committee and share options for consideration of member states. Chair, as a practical manifestation of our commitment to the efficiency drive, Pakistan has decided to biennialize its two resolutions in the regional disarmament cluster. We hope that this step would not only contribute to improving efficacy of the FES committee, but also be reciprocated positively by member states through their continued support to these initiatives. I thank you, Chair.
I thank the distinguished representative of Pakistan. Now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Maldives.

Thank you, Chair. I congratulate you and members of the Bureau on your election. You will have the full support of the Maldives. Let me also thank the Bureau for the careful work undertaken to organize this session. For a small delegation, working methods determine our ability to participate meaningfully. We suggest three areas for attention. First, predictability. Rolling speakers list and changes to the schedule may sometimes be necessary, but reasonable notice matters. There should also be sufficient time between circulation of drafts, consultations and action. For smaller delegations, compressed timeline can mean fewer opportunities to engage with substance. Second, The first committee does not operate in isolation. Important parts of disarmament architecture are based in Geneva and Vienna. Not every delegation can maintain a specialist to cover all three duty stations. We therefore encourage better connectivity between these processes. Before each session, the secretariat could provide a concise mapping of relevant documents in Geneva, Vienna, and elsewhere against the committee's thematic clusters. with briefers and documents readily accessible to delegations in New York. Within the committee, we support a single user-friendly digital platform, bringing together current draft texts, revisions, consultation schedules, and status of action. New initiatives should also be discussed early enough for delegations to genuinely shape them. Third, accountability. This year's arrangements are exceptional. And at the end of the session, a short assessment could identify what worked, where process errors, and what lessons could inform future sessions. On program planning, agreed mandates must have the resources needed for effective implementation. Planning should strengthen delivery of these mandates, not reopen decisions already taken by member states. For the most Good working methods means every delegation, regardless of size or capacity, has the realistic opportunity to follow, negotiate, and contribute. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Maldives. Now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Denmark.

Thank you, Chair. Let me start by congratulating you on your election as chair of the First Committee. is looking forward to working with you and the entire Bureau, and I can assure you of our full cooperation and support. Chair, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, as we start our deliberations in the First Committee this year, we welcome the proposals on the working methods, the programme of work and the timetable with the measures taken. We find the proposals are a useful basis as a compromise between different positions for our work over the coming weeks. They will improve our work, and we can support them. In the proposals, we specifically appreciate the speaking times in the general debate are kept as last year. The use of automatic microphone cutoff has been retained, the lower number of sessions allocated, and retaining the initiative on information on states requiring votes. Denmark fully recognizes progress in efficiencies made over the most recent 1C sessions, but we would, however, like to have seen further tightening of the framework this year. which could have been done without compromising our deliberations, state positions, further politicizations or outcomes. As such, tightening of the framework will not increase differences between states or cause more votes. Differences between states and call for votes are expression of different political positions, which honestly is not solved by longer or more statements in this room. Chair, in line with the 1C Franco-German non-paper, which we fully support, and all Member State statements, except one, as I recall it, during the intercessional informal discussion on working methods, which we highly appreciated, we continue to see merit in shorter time for statements in the general debate, the thematic debates, and right of reply. We also see merit in a merger of some of the clusters. And as a small delegation, we would welcome such action. And actually, you're looking at the Danish delegation right now. Rights of reply should be brief, to the point and concise. They should not be a repetition or continuation of a statement already delivered, but address a specific point. And we should hear rights of reply at the end of each of the thematic debates. And an observation from our side which continues to puzzle us is to have right of reply in the thematic debates that are longer than the speaking time for the statement does not make sense. The time for right of reply should be calibrated. Progress on arms control, disarmament and non-proliferation is not done primarily through the formal and pre-scripted statements or rights of reply here. That is not real, substantive dialogue, and I underline dialogue, and does not lead to outcomes in itself. Our scarce time is better spent in informal consultation on the text we have in front of us and on finding common ground and compromises in order to reach results and outcomes. Finally, we also join the call to penholders to take a careful look at resolutions before tabling them, while of course recognizing the right of states to table them. What is the purpose of the text and what is the purpose of tabling the text? Is it necessary to table a text every year or could it wait until there are substantial changes? Could it be a decision instead? Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Denmark. Now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Islamic Republic of Iran.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. Enhancing the effectiveness of the United Nations cannot be achieved through organizational and procedural changes. It requires restoring confidence and trust in the organization through full adherence to international law. and the UN Charter, principles that have been violated, particularly over the past two years, by certain members in a grave and systematic manner and with impunity. We also believe that the primary cause of the organization's current liquidity crisis, which has led to the launch of the UN80 initiative, is the chronic late payment of assessed contributions by the largest contributor of the organization. The difficulties facing disarmament forums stem primarily from the lack of political will, the reluctance of certain states to engage in dialogue based on equality, mutual respect, and sovereign equality, and attempts to instrumentalize multilateral mechanisms for political purposes. Organizational issues should not be invoked to divert attention from these root causes. We consider that the established method of works of the first committee remain effective and don't require revision. The changes introduced last year were exceptional measures and should not establish a precedent for the committee's current and future work. Those changes have had unintended consequences, including the dilution of substantive discussions, by reducing statements to a brief and unelaborated positions and transforming meaningful exchanges into procedural formalities. The superficial consideration of complex security issues can deepen misunderstanding and mistrust, thereby diminishing the prospect for consensus. The Committee should therefore return to its established practice regarding the number of meetings, the length of statements during the general debate and the thematic discussions, and the exercise of right of reply. We support voluntary discipline in the length of statements rather than rigid time limits. The number of resolutions and decisions reflects the diversity of member states' priorities and is an essential expression of multilateralism. We support voluntary efforts by sponsors to streamline initiatives, but reject arbitrary caps or pressure that could marginalize national and regional concerns. Such efforts must remain member state driven and respect the prerogative of sponsors. Mr. Chair, with your indulgence, I request one additional minute to raise a point of order. I am obliged to draw the kind attention of you and the distinguished delegations to a serious situation concerning the continuing failure of the host country to issue visas to Iranian representatives who were scheduled to attend the meeting.
I thank the disarmament representative of Iran. Now I give the floor to the disarmament representative of Egypt.

A few months ago, you were faced by a major setback to our disarmament machinery, which is the third consecutive failure to reach an outcome document for our NPT Review Conference. This is both a clear depiction of the weakened state of our machinery a wake-up call that reform is needed. Coming from a developing country, we do not like trickle-down approaches. We favor more bottom-up reforms. Practically, this means that we need to start with the grassroots, which is our working methods. For Egypt, tackling working methods shall be done with the understanding that cutting down the duration of our statements is is not because we don't want to work. It's rather because time is precious. It has an opportunity cost, which is doing the real work that matters. In brief, this means the following. We need more informants and less statements. Second, through fewer and clustered rights of replies, we're recalibrating the balance of our committee to the technical and practical aspects rather than the political rhetoric. Third, changing the periodicity of the resolutions to being biennial and triennial shall open the door for newer resolutions to be presented, resolutions that tackle the core reasons for why our disarmament machinery is lagging behind. We should seek options to practically implement the NPT in a balanced manner, to bring discussions of emerging technologies, ICT, AI, military domain under the umbrella of the UN, among other things. Simply, Chair, Reforming our working methods is the first step to an agile and effective First Committee. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Egypt. Now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Singapore.

Thank you very much, Chair. Let me begin by congratulating you and members of the Bureau on your election. My delegation is confident that under your leadership, we'll bring our work to a successful conclusion. I wish to make two points on the working methods of our committee. First, we have to make a serious effort at this session to further streamline our work and improve our working methods. The First Committee adopts more resolutions by vote than any other main committee. This imposes a heavy burden, especially on small delegations. The UN80 reform exercise gives us an additional reason to improve our working methods. We would strongly recommend to all delegations to make a start by reducing the length of resolutions and also by introducing review clauses for new resolutions where appropriate. Additionally, we would also support the biennializing and triennializing of annual resolutions. As we improve our working methods, it is equally important that we adopt an approach that is even-handed and that is applied across the board. Second, we must continue to enhance transparency in the work of our Committee. In this regard, delegations will recall that Singapore and South Africa had jointly introduced decision 79/516, entitled Information on Requests for Votes, at the 79th session in 2024. The objective of this resolution was simple, to improve transparency and facilitate the flow of information among member states. We believe that enhancing transparency in our work is essential to build confidence, encourage meaningful dialogue, and strengthen the credibility of our work. My delegation calls on you, the Chair, Excellency, to continue with the implementation of this resolution at this session. This year, pursuant to the decision 79/516, Singapore, together with South Africa and also a group of Member States, we intend to submit a formal request calling on the Chair to continue the practice of providing information on the identity of the Member States that requested a vote on draft resolution or decisions tabled for action in this Committee or their specific paragraphs. In conclusion, I wish to underline that working methods is not just a question of time management and reducing the number of resolutions. Ultimately, working methods are a means to build trust, enhance transparency, and strengthen mutual understanding. And most importantly, by improving our working methods, we can deliver meaningful and much-needed results. Singapore stands ready to work constructively with all Member States in this regard. And we also take this opportunity, Mr. Chair, to extend to you our support to your program of work and to your efforts to find a pragmatic solution on this issue so that we can proceed very efficiently with the rest of our work. Thank you very much.
I thank the distinguished representative of Singapore. Now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Turkey.

Thank you, Chair, and courtesies on behalf of the Czech delegation.

Distinguished delegates, colleagues, friends, allow me to voice our strong support for the programme of.

Work as proposed by the Bureau and for the revitalisation efforts clearly reflected in this draft. We, however, believe that the potential of these efforts has not been fully utilised. The Czech Republic echoes views expressed by many delegations that revitalization should not be about cutting just for the sake of cutting, but about minimalizing duplications, avoiding overlaps, and ensuring a more streamlined and focused program of work. Effectiveness is not simply characterized by the number of meeting days, but rather how we fill them. By cutting unnecessary statements, reducing the length and frequency of rights of replies, minimizing technical rollover resolutions, and promoting thereby or triannualization in accordance with the UN80 initiative, we can promote increasingly focused debates. A more effective first committee is not only a matter of efficiency. At a time when the international community expects this committee to respond to real and growing challenges, streamlining and revitalizing our work is a simple matter of credibility. Chair, we do not share the view of some delegations that in the reaction to revitalization of work of the First Committee, our mutual distrust increased, while the number of consensual resolutions decreased. There are other long-standing causes for such an unfortunate trend. Similarly, politization of our debates cannot be blamed on UN80. We indeed agree that in the current geopolitical situation, collective efforts based on dialogue and diplomacy remain the most significant tool for maintaining regional and international security. They must be, however, approached honestly, collaboratively, and without malicious intent. I thank you, Chair.
I thank the distinguished representative of Turkey. Now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Tajikistan.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. First of all, allow me on behalf of the Tajikistan, uh, the delegation of Tajikistan to congratulate you, uh, and the members of the Bureau on your election. You can count on Tajikistan's full support for your work and for your efforts. in guiding the First Committee during the 81st session of the GA. Mr. Chair, Tajikistan attaches great importance to the effective work of the First Committee. At the same time, we believe that improving its work's methods should preserve the key principles guiding the General Assembly. In this regard, my delegation welcomes the opportunity to discuss practical ways to make the work of the committee more effective. We believe that timely distribution of documents is very important. Early circulation of draft resolutions and other relevant documents gives all delegations enough time to study them and to hold consultations. We also support efforts to reduce unnecessary duplication in the work of the committee. Where possible, better coordination of relevant agenda items and thematic clusters could help us use our time more effectively. At the same time, such measures should not reduce the substance of our discussions or limit the ability of Member States to raise issues that are important to their national and regional priorities. Tajikistan also attaches great importance to having enough time for informal consultation. consultations. Mr. Chair, we are aware of the financial and resource challenges facing the UN. At the same time, we believe that improving efficiency should not affect the ability of the organization to carry out the mandates given to it by member states. In this regard, Tajikistan supports a balanced, gradual, and consensus-based approach to improving the working methods of the First Committee. Mr. Chair, the First Committee remains one of the main structures of the UN dealing with disarmament and international security. In today's increasingly complex international environment, our common goal should be to make its work more effective while keeping it an inclusive platform for dialogue and discussion. Tajikistan stands ready to work constructively with all delegations and the Bureau in this regard. Thank you, Mr. Chair.
I thank the distinguished representative of Tajikistan. Now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of the United States of America.

The United States welcomes this opportunity to address the working methods of the first committee. Over the past year, this committee has seen clear evidence that it can work more efficiently, more deliberately, and at lower cost without sacrificing substance or participation. Even with a shorter schedule and tighter speaking limits, participation remained strong, interventions remained robust, and the committee fulfilled its mandate. No delegation was denied the opportunity to be heard, and no convincing case has been made that the committee was unable to do its work. That matters because this discussion is not about procedure for its own sake. It is about whether the committee is willing to match its practices to its actual workload, respect the time and resources of member states, and contribute to a more effective and accountable United Nations. We believe the committee should continue moving towards shorter, more disciplined sessions, more reasonable speaking limits, and a more focused use of conference time. Every additional day, every unnecessary intervention, and every avoidable resolution carries a cost. If the work can be done in less time, then it should be. That same principle applies to rights of reply. They serve a legitimate function, but they should not become a vehicle for extending debate indefinitely or for restating national positions at greater length than the original statements themselves. If this committee is serious about discipline, then rights of reply should be limited accordingly. The same principle applies to resolutions. Too many return year after year with little or no substantive change. We welcome those delegations that have responded constructively to calls for longer periodicity, not a word you use very often, but others have not. Annual consideration of resolutions that do not require annual action wastes time and resources. The committee should focus its attention on new proposals and texts that require genuine negotiation, rather than repeatedly spending the same effort on texts with technical updates or minimal changes. The United States recognizes that not every delegation supports reform with the same urgency. And man, we see this all over the UN. But the evidence is clear and the need for change is no longer in doubt. This committee can work more efficiently and it should. We remain committed to working constructively to advance practical reforms, but we also expect this process to deliver more than discussion. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of USA. Now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Algeria.

Thank you, Chair. Algeria aligns itself with the statement delivered by Namibia on behalf of the African Group. Three points. First, on transparency, we wish to express once again our sincere appreciation and support to Singapore and South Africa for the decision 79/516, which marked a significant step forward in enhancing the transparency and predictability of our work. To illustrate why this decision is important, allow me to share a concrete national experience. Algeria submits annually a draft resolution entitled Strengthening Security and Cooperation in the Mediterranean. Historically, this text was adopted by consensus. However, in 2018, despite the resolution undergoing limited changes, a delegation suddenly requested a recorded vote, without prior notice, without raising any explicit or implicit substantive concerns, and without any direct relation to the text itself. What followed was a frustrating struggle simply to identify which delegation had called for the vote. Colleagues, When consensus is broken anonymously on a technically updated text, it creates unnecessary ambiguity and undermines trust. Knowing we request a recorded vote is not about assigning blame. It is about procedural fairness, transparency, and dialogue. Second point, regarding speaking time limits, further reducing allocated time risk diminishing the quality and substance of our deliberations. The Algerian delegation has usually quite short statements. But we respect the right of everyone to articulate orally and fully their positions. To address this, we could urge delegations to keep their remarks within a set timeframe without pressuring them to condense their points beyond what is practical from their perspective. Third and last point regarding the resolution's periodicity. This should be considered on a case-by-case basis and by consensus. Technical updates should not be the criteria, or at least not the only criteria to make such decision. Thank you, Chair, and I give 38 seconds to the following delegations.
Thank you. I thank the distinguished representative of Algeria. Now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Nigeria.

Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Nigeria aligns itself with the statement delivered by Namibia on behalf of the African Group and wishes to have a few brief remarks. My delegation congratulates you, Mr. Chair, and other members of the Bureau on your election and assure you of Nigeria's full support and cooperation. We also appreciate the Bureau effort to ensure an orderly, balanced, efficient program of work for the committee. Nigeria support practical measures aimed at improving efficiency of the first committee. However, efficiency should not be pursued at the expense of substantive engagement, inclusiveness, or the ability of member states to participate meaningfully in the committee work. In particular, Nigeria attach importance to preserving adequate time for the general debate and thematic cluster debates. This segment provide an essential opportunity for delegation to set national priority, respond to evolving security challenges, and contribute substantively across the broad range of disarmament and international security issues before the Committee. This is especially important for developing countries and delegations with limited personnel, which most often cover several thematic areas simultaneously. Working method reform should therefore take into consideration the differing capacity of delegation and should not inadvertently narrow the space available for effective participation. Nigeria also of a view that it's important to maintain appropriate balance between substantive deliberations and procedural intervention. Right of reply, explanation of vote, and other procedural mechanism remain legitimate and necessary, but their use should not unduly displace the time available for substantive consideration of committee agenda. Nigeria further emphasizes that any significant adjustment to established working methods should be transparent, consultative, and broadly supported by member states. Predictability and inclusiveness remain essential to preserving confidence in the committee procedures. Finally, Mr. Chair, Nigeria will continue to engage constructively with you, the Bureau, and all delegation in support of a first committee that is efficient in its method, inclusive in its participation, and substantive in its outcome. I thank you, Mr. Chair.
I thank the distinguished representative of Nigeria. Now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Netherlands.

Mr. Chair, thank you for giving me the floor. Let me first congratulate you on your election as chair. Please be assured of the support and cooperation of the delegation of the Kingdom of the Netherlands to work with you, the bureau, the secretariats, and all delegations. Mr. Chair, the Netherlands firmly stands for the important work that we do here. The First Committee is and remains at the heart of multilateral work on matters of international peace and security. With regard to the programme of work and timetable, as well as the working methods, the Netherlands commend you, the Bureau and the Secretariat for the work done. I'd like to confirm our support for what you have presented to us as a proposal that emerged after lengthy discussions. In our view, the efficiencies you present are fitting of where the UN finds itself. In the year following the start of the UN80 initiative, it is only logical that the First Committee too is subject to a discussion and proposals on streamlining. Mr. Chair, as other delegations have pointed out, revitalizing the disarmament machinery is not only about the practice of imposing time limits on the First Committee for the sake of cutting time. Rather, we believe it is important to also critically examine the ways in which we work, on the frequency of annual resolutions, the number of meetings, and the way we organize the right of reply. Such examinations and actions should go beyond the First Committee. We look with concern at what is happening, or I should say what is not happening, in the Conference on Disarmament in Geneva, as an example. As we mark our 30th year in that forum without substantive negotiations, it is important that we improve its functioning. Until we are able to do so, we would prefer to organise that work in a way that is more proportionate to its outcome. Mr. Chair, looking ahead, we stand ready to work on the basis of your proposal this year, but believe there are further steps to be taken in revitalizing the disarmament machinery. We look forward to discuss these steps this year and in the year to come. I thank you, Mr. Chair.
I thank the distinguished representative of the Netherlands. Now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Ghana.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Mr. Chair, at the onset, allow me to extend my delegation's warm congratulations to you on your election, as well as the other members of your Bureau, and assure you of Ghana's full support and constructive cooperation. Ghana aligns itself with the statement delivered on behalf of the Group of African States and the Movement of Non-Aligned Countries, and wish to make the following remarks in its national capacity. Against the backdrop of the 81st session's theme, restoring trust, managing transformation, global military expenditure has surged to an unprecedented 2.9 trillion US dollars. This staggering allocation highlights a critical security paradox, massive investment of arms have not fortified collective stability, but rather intensified geopolitical friction while starving sustainable development. For Ghana, disarmament is not an abstract ideal, but a practical imperative for the protection of human life, To translate this imperative to action, my delegation will focus on three core priorities: restoring trust in the nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation regime, protecting people from weapons that cause daily loss of life, and managing the security implications of emerging technologies. As a party to the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons, Ghana was honored to host the regional conference on its universalization in Accra in January this year. Ghana considered the TPNW to complement and reinforce the NPT, and we look forward to a successful first review conference of the treaty in December. My delegation also reaffirms its steadfast commitment to the African Nuclear Weapon Free Zone Treaty of PIDB. We also continue to support the establishment of a free zone nuclear weapons of all other weapons of mass destruction in the Middle East. Mr. Chairman, in West Africa, the immediate human security acutely threatened by illicit proliferation of small arms and light weapons and improvised explosive devices driven by terrorists, criminal networks to counter insecurity spreading from the Sahel to the coastal states. Ghana proactively through the initiative of the National Commission on Small Arms and Light Weapons at the national level, a Ghana amnesty program from the 1st of December 2025 to the 30th of January 2026.
I thank the distinguished representative of Ghana. Now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Equatorial Guinea.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Allow me at the outset to congratulate you on your election. I also wish to congratulate the other members of the Bureau. Chair, Equatorial Guinea aligns itself with the statement made by Namibia on behalf of the African Group. My delegation is of the view that improving the working methods of the First Committee must be done in such a way as to strike a balance between effectiveness and the right of delegations to adequately express their views. With this in mind, we are of the view that it is important to retain reasonable time limits for oral statements. Written statements published on the portal are a useful tool, but they should not substitute a verbal exchange of views between delegations. If speaking times cease to be relevant, it could be reduced to one minute, or we could simply hold debates by mail. We're here precisely in order to express our positions, to listen to each other, and to engage in dialogue. We should also underscore the importance here of multilingualism. This issue is not solely one that pertains to or affects formal meetings. In several consultations, in informal consultations, the lack of interpretation can stymie the ability of some delegations whose working language is not English to participate fully. or to make proposals or to react to proposals on an equal footing with their counterparts, the quest for effectiveness should not ultimately and involuntarily translate into an advantage for some delegations over others on linguistic grounds. Multilingualism is also an issue of effective and inclusive participation. For this reason, any improvement made to our working methods should preserve the quality of our discussions, as well as reasonable speaking times and, insofar as possible, linguistic conditions which allow the effective participation of all delegations. Thank you, Chair.
I thank the distinguished representative of Equatorial Guinea. And now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of India.

Thank you, Mr. Chair, and good afternoon, colleagues. India congratulates the friendly and neighborly country of Nepal, and you in particular, Mr. Chair, and all the members of the Bureau on your election. Mr. Chair, trust, the core currency of the multilateral system, is becoming scarcer with each passing day. We must be clear that to build trust, a UN that delivers for all, requires substantive, not procedural, reforms. These reforms should begin where the need is the greatest, crucially, the Security Council, whose reform has remained in abeyance for far too long. Strengthening its inclusivity is essential to the credibility and legitimacy of the UN as a whole, including the First Committee. Mr. Chair, the UN comprises many bodies, each with working methods suited to its role. This is equally true of the disarmament machinery, where the Conference on Disarmament, the Disarmament Commission, and this Committee reflect distinct mandates. As one of the GS' oldest standing bodies, this Committee has developed working methods that enable all States, regardless of size or influence, to engage as equals on international peace and security matters. Mr. Chair, India has long supported improving working methods across the multilateral system, including here. We have noted the various suggestions, many of which merit careful and balanced consideration. On the debate on working methods, my delegation has the following three points to make. First, while we support streamlining working methods and ensuring that time allotted to this committee is corresponding to its allocated work, statements should remain a meaningful exchange, not merely a procedural exercise. Resolutions play an important role in shaping and clarifying opinio juris and state practice, and thereby contribute to the development of international law. In this context, the implications of reducing the frequency deserve careful attention. Third, on de-anonymizing votes, my delegation notes that while greater disclosure may promote openness, however, it could make it harder for smaller delegations to express divergent views, risk further politicization, and shift attention from substance to procedure. Mr. Chair, India's view is that this committee's current working methods have served it well and remain relevant. We also share the objective of strengthening and reforming them and believe that a pragmatic, measured, and inclusive approach would best achieve it. I thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of India. We have just heard the last speaker in the debate on agenda items 124 and 139. The President of the General Assembly will address the committee at that meeting. After opening statement and prior to the general debate, the committee will resume its considerations of its program of work. It's contained in document S/C1/81/CRP1. I intend to hold consultations on this document 15 PM this afternoon in conference room 12 and all interested delegations are invited to attend. I look forward to working closely with you, all of you, in the coming weeks. The meeting is adjourned.
